Question 2

library(dplyr)
flights_times <- flights |>
  mutate(
    dep_time_clean = dep_time %% 2400,
    arr_time_clean = arr_time %% 2400,
    
    dep_category = case_when(
      dep_time_clean < 600  ~ "early morning",
      dep_time_clean < 1200 ~ "morning",
      dep_time_clean < 1800 ~ "afternoon",
      dep_time_clean < 2400 ~ "evening",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    arr_category = case_when(
      arr_time_clean < 600  ~ "early morning",
      arr_time_clean < 1200 ~ "morning",
      arr_time_clean < 1800 ~ "afternoon",
      arr_time_clean < 2400 ~ "evening",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

time_levels <- c(
  "early morning",
  "morning",
  "afternoon",
  "evening"
)

flights_times <- flights_times |>
  mutate(
    dep_category = factor(dep_category, levels = time_levels),
    arr_category = factor(arr_category, levels = time_levels)
  )

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(
  data = flights_times,
  aes(x = dep_category)
) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Flights by Departure Time",
    x = "Departure Time Category",
    y = "Number of Flights"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(
  data = flights_times,
  aes(x = arr_category)
) +
  geom_bar(fill = "darkorange") +
  labs(
    title = "Flights by Arrival Time",
    x = "Arrival Time Category",
    y = "Number of Flights"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
flights_times <- flights_times |>
  mutate(
    red_eye = dep_category %in% c("afternoon", "evening") &
      arr_category %in% c("early morning", "morning")
  )

red_eye_summary <- flights_times |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_category), !is.na(arr_category)) |>
  summarize(
    total_flights = n(),
    red_eye_flights = sum(red_eye),
    red_eye_percentage = mean(red_eye) * 100
  )

red_eye_summary
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  total_flights red_eye_flights red_eye_percentage
          <int>           <int>              <dbl>
1        328063           10754               3.28
  1. When looking at the bar plot for departure time. We can see that most flights departed in the morning or in the afternoon, both a little under 125000 flights. A big chunk, about 75000 flights, departed in the evening. Only a very small amount of flights departed in the early morning, and about the same amount was classified as NA. When looking at arrival time, most flights arrived in the evening. Then, the afternoon and morning had the most arrivals, in that order. Very little flights arrived in the early morning, and about the same amount was classified as NA. Out of the 328063 total flights, 10754 were red eye flights, which corresponds to 3.278% of all flights.

Question 4

There is a missing relationship between weather and airports. The missing relationship is between faa in airports and origin in the weather dataset. The origin variable in the weather dataset identifies where each weather observation was recorded, which corresponds to the faa variable in the airports dataset. Thus, there should be a branch airports$faa, with an arrow to weather$origin.

There are 3 duplicate IDs, they occurred on November 3rd, 2013. On this date, daylight saving ended. Since the time moved an hour back, 1:00 am occurred twice at each airport. The pasted ID cannot distinguish them, while time_hour stores them as two separate moments.

The head and tail functions show the first and last 6 rows of the dataset, respectively. It gives us all the observations. When looking at the first 6 rows, it is data from the first day of the first month in 2013. It is chronologically ordered by departure time. It also shows us the scheduled departure time, and any delays, and then all the same things with arrival as well. It also gives us a lot of information about the weather. When looking at the first 6 rows of the dataset, nothings seems corrupted that would have to be removed. The last 6 rows contain data from September 30th of 2013. There is no data that looks weird, so nothing has to be removed.

weather_long <- flights_weather |>
  select(
    temp,
    dewp,
    humid,
    wind_speed,
    wind_gust,
    precip,
    pressure,
    visib
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "weather_variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(value))

ggplot(
  data = weather_long,
  aes(x = value)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "seagreen",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~weather_variable,
    scales = "free"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distributions of Weather Measurements",
    x = "Observed value",
    y = "Number of flights"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

When looking at the distribution for the departure delays, the data is heavily right skewed. This means that most flights departed either on time, slightly delayed, or earlier than scheduled, and that very few flights had long delays. When looking at the distribution for arrival delays, it shows that this distribution is also heavily right skewed. Most flights arrived either early, on time, or there was a very slight delay. Only a small number of flights arrived very delayed.

When looking at the distribution of weather measurements, there are different plots for the different variables. Precipitation is very concentrated at 0, meaning that most flights departed with no precipitation. Visibility is concentrated at 10 miles, meaning that most flights had maximum visibility. Pressure is approximately bell shaped around 1015. Both wind speed and gust are right skewed. Temperature, dew point, and humidity all have a wide range.

Question 7

delay_data <- flights_weather |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_delay)) |>
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(
      time_hour,
      tz = "America/New_York"
    )
  )

daily_delays <- delay_data |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarize(
    average_dep_delay = mean(dep_delay),
    number_of_flights = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(average_dep_delay))

worst_day <- daily_delays |>
  slice_max(
    average_dep_delay,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

daily_origin_delays <- delay_data |>
  group_by(date, origin) |>
  summarize(
    average_dep_delay = mean(dep_delay),
    number_of_flights = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(average_dep_delay))

worst_airport_day <- daily_origin_delays |>
  slice_max(

library(nycflights13)
library(leaflet)

destination_delays <- flights |>
  group_by(dest) |>
  summarize(
    average_arr_delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    number_of_flights = sum(!is.na(arr_delay)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

airports_delays <- airports |>
  left_join(
    destination_delays,
    by = c("faa" = "dest")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(average_arr_delay))

delay_colors <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "RdYlBu",
  domain = airports_delays$average_arr_delay,
  reverse = TRUE
)

leaflet(data = airports_delays) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~lon,
    lat = ~lat,
    radius = 6,
    color = ~delay_colors(average_arr_delay),
    fillColor = ~delay_colors(average_arr_delay),
    fillOpacity = 0.8,
    stroke = FALSE,
    label = ~paste0(
      name,
      " (", faa, ")",
      ": ",
      round(average_arr_delay, 1),
      " minute average arrival delay"
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    position = "bottomright",
    pal = delay_colors,
    values = ~average_arr_delay,
    title = "Average arrival<br>delay (minutes)",
    opacity = 1
  )

# Correlation for weather variables without wind direction because its circular
weather_correlations <- delay_weather |>
  summarize(
    across(
      c(
        temp,
        dewp,
        humid,
        wind_speed,
        wind_gust,
        precip,
        pressure,
        visib
      ),
      ~cor(dep_delay, .x, use = "complete.obs")
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "weather_variable",
    values_to = "correlation"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(correlation)))

When looking at the graph ‘average departure delay by temperature,’ we can see how average departure delay varied across different temperatures. We can see that the average departure delay is the lowest around 47 degrees Fahrenheit. Anything colder than this has average delays around 11 minutes. At temperatures above this point, the average departure delay generally increased. There was a big spike in delay between approximately 72 and 76 degrees Fahrenheit. The highest temperature group was associated with the longest average departure delay.

When looking at the graph including dew point, we can see that the average departure delay remained fairly consistent up to approximately 30 degrees Fahrenheit. Around 32 degrees, the average departure delay increased to almost 12 minutes. It then decreased around 39 degrees before generally increasing as the dew point rose further. The largest increase in average departure delay occurred at the highest dew point values.

When looking at the graph including average relative humidity, we can see that average departure delay remained relatively low when average relative humidity was below approximately 60%. Above 60% humidity, average departure delay generally increased. The increase was especially large at the highest humidity levels, with the highest average relative humidity being associated with an average departure delay of approximately 25 minutes. Therefore, higher humidity was associated with longer average departure delays.

When looking at the graph including wind direction, we can see that South East winds were associated with the longest average departure delay at approximately 18 minutes. East and South winds were also associated with relatively long average delays of approximately 17 minutes. North West winds were associated with the shortest average delay at approximately 9 minutes. Overall, average departure delays varied depending on wind direction.

When looking at the plot with the wind conditions, we can see that the average departure delay with low winds was about 11 minutes, with moderate wind about 13 minutes, and with strong wind about 17 minutes. Thus, stronger winds were associated with longer average departure delays.

When looking at the plot with average wind gust, we can see that average departure delay fluctuates across the lower and moderate wind gust values. There is a noticeable increase in average delay between approximately 22 and 24 mph, followed by a decrease between approximately 25 and 28 mph. The strongest wind gust group, at approximately 38 mph, was associated with the longest average departure delay at approximately 19 minutes. Overall, stronger wind gusts were generally associated with longer departure delays, although this relationship was not completely consistent.

When looking at the plot with precipitation condition and average delay, we can see that the average delay with heavy precipitation is approximately 41 minutes, with light precipitation approximately 29 minutes, and with no precipitation about 11 minutes. Thus, heavier precipitation was associated with longer average departure delays.

When looking at the graph with atmospheric pressure, we can see that lower atmospheric pressure were associated with longer average departure delays. The two lowest pressure groups, at approximately 1005 and 1010 millibars, had average delays of about 19 minutes. As atmospheric pressure increased, the average departure delay generally decreased. The highest pressure group, at approximately 1031 millibars, was associated with the the shortest average delay of about 6 minutes.

When looking at the plot with visibility conditions, the average departure delay with clear visibility was approximately 11 minutes, with low visibility approximately 25 minutes, and with reduced visibility approximately 20 minutes. This suggests that worse visibility was associated with longer average departure delays.

The last graph plots the correlation coefficients between departure delay and each weather variable. Both visibility and pressure have a negative correlation with departure delay, meaning that if visibility or pressure increases, departure delay generally decreases. Humidity has the strongest correlation coefficient of 0.117. Among the variables with positive correlations, humidity was followed by dew point, precipitation, temperature, wind speed, and wind gust. Wind direction was not included in the correlation analysis because it is a circular variable.

After looking at all the graphs, we can conclude that precipitation showed the largest difference in average departure delay. High humidity, high dew point, low atmospheric pressure, low visibility, and strong winds were also associated with longer average delays. Southeast winds were associated with the longest average delay among the wind directions. However, because all correlation coefficients were weak, weather conditions alone do not explain departure delays. There are other factors that might also be associated with departure delays.
